# 12. Running nodes and servers for a Kaspa app

The unglamorous part. Every item here took a wallet, a watcher or a payment flow down at least once, Sept 2025 to Nov 2026. rusty-kaspa 2.1.0 unless stated.

## 1. Public nodes, the REST API, or your own node

**Most apps do not need their own node.** If your server holds no key (the user's wallet signs), public infrastructure is enough. See the tiers in `00-agent-rules.md`, "How strict to be".

Public sources (Nov 2026):

- **Public nodes through the SDK's `Resolver`.** The WASM SDK picks a public node for you: `new kaspa.RpcClient({ resolver: new kaspa.Resolver(), networkId: 'mainnet' })`, then `await rpc.connect()` (the pattern of rusty-kaspa's own examples, `wasm/examples`). Check `getInfo()` for `isSynced` and `isUtxoIndexed` before relying on it, and reconnect through the resolver when a node drops.
- **The REST API at api.kaspa.org.** Address balances, UTXOs, transactions and their history, block times, the KAS price (`/info/price`). Docs at api.kaspa.org/docs. It is backed by archival nodes, so it can serve old transactions a pruned node cannot. It is rate-limited: cache answers, and back off on 429.
- **Prices.** For the KAS price: CoinGecko or api.kaspa.org `/info/price`. For KCC-20 tokens: CoinGecko lists some (NACHO is there); kascov.io reports prices calculated from the pools it can see (`https://kascov.io/data/<network>/…`). Name the source and the time next to every price, and show "unavailable" when the sources fail (`09-verify-and-read-the-chain.md` section 5).
- **Testnet-10** (the live Toccata testnet): faucet `https://faucet-tn10.kaspanet.io`, explorer `https://explorer-tn10.kaspa.org`, REST API `https://api-tn10.kaspa.org` (as listed on wiki.kaspa.org/en/testnets; check they answer before sending a user there). Testnet addresses start with `kaspatest:`.

Run your own node when:

- your server holds a key or users' money (`11-hot-keys-signers-watchers.md`);
- you run a watcher, an indexer or a keeper that must not go blind when a public node does;
- you need `subscribeUtxosChanged` on many addresses, the full virtual chain, or a rate no public service gives you.

The rest of this section is for running your own:

- Build kaspad from source at a release tag and keep the WASM SDK from the same release (`02-sending-and-signing-kas.md`).
- **`--utxoindex` is required** for `getUtxosByAddresses`, balance queries and `subscribeUtxosChanged`. Without it, address subscriptions do not work.
- RPC listeners: `--rpclisten=<ip>:16110` (gRPC), `--rpclisten-borsh=<ip>:17110` (wRPC Borsh), `--rpclisten-json=<ip>:18110` (wRPC JSON). Bind to `127.0.0.1` for anything only the same box uses.
- **Borsh is version-coupled; JSON is not.** A WASM SDK one release behind the node connects, answers `getInfo`, subscribes, then drops on the first notification it cannot decode, and reconnects forever. Match the SDK to the node, or use the JSON wRPC if you want something that survives node upgrades. (Proven on mainnet at the Toccata upgrade, June 2026.)
- **The node accepts 128 RPC clients by default.** A public node fills that up with strangers' wallets and bots, and then refuses your own app ("reached connection capacity of 128" in `journalctl -u kaspad`). Your app sends then hang in "syncing". Raise it with `--rpcmaxclients=1024`, or firewall the RPC ports to your own boxes. Check with `journalctl -u kaspad --since "-30 min" --no-pager | grep -c "connection capacity"`. (Proven on mainnet, Oct 2026.)
- **Your own app can exhaust it too.** A send path that opened a new gRPC connection per transaction and never closed it filled the node and made every later send time out. Use one shared connection per process, with a timeout on every call.
- **DNS seeders are not RPC servers.** A wallet library defaulted to `seeder1.kaspad.net:16110` for RPC; sends hung. Point every client at a node you chose, in one constant, and check which constant the running code actually reads.
- Decide which node is public and which is private. Keep the node your money paths depend on firewalled to your own boxes; offer a different one to the community if you want to.
- Upgrades: `git fetch --tags`, check out the release tag, `cargo build --release --bin kaspad`, restart the unit, follow `journalctl -u kaspad -f`. Know which binary your systemd unit runs; a stray copy in `/usr/local/bin` is a classic confusion.
- Testnet: testnet-10 is the live Toccata testnet (Nov 2026). If you run your own testnet node, run it as its own unit with its own data dir and ports (for example gRPC 16210, Borsh 17210, JSON 18210, P2P 16211) so it never collides with mainnet.

## 2. Disk

- Old node data directories are huge. A cleanup on one box found about 350 GB of stale node data from replaced units.
- MySQL binary logs grew to 45 GB on an indexer box. Set an expiry (`binlog_expire_logs_seconds`, 2 days is plenty for most) unless you need point-in-time recovery.
- Flush process-manager logs on a schedule. A full disk stops the node, the database and the watcher at the same moment.

## 3. Process manager and environment

- After changing an environment variable, check that the running process has it. `pm2 restart <app> --update-env` did not reach the process once; deleting and starting it fresh did.
- If a module reads `process.env` at require time, `dotenv.config()` must run before that module is first required. A constant that ignores `.env` is usually this.
- A deploy service run with `NODE_ENV=production` passed it to its child `npm install`, which silently skipped devDependencies; every build that needed TypeScript failed for a week. Strip `NODE_ENV` from child processes or use `npm install --include=dev` for builds.
- Wrap every long node call (wallet sync, chain read) in a timeout. A sync promise that never resolved sat in a "sync in progress" map forever, every later send waited on it, and the reverse proxy returned 504 to every user (`13-node-error-messages.md`, "Unexpected token '<'").
- Run public apps as their own users, not root. Keep the signer, key service and watcher on boxes that serve nothing else public.

## 4. Cloudflare and TLS

- **API and signer subdomains: DNS only (grey cloud).** A proxied record put Cloudflare's challenge page in front of an API, and every non-browser client broke. Proxy the website; leave machine-facing hosts unproxied or add rules that skip challenges.
- **SSL mode must be Full (strict)**, not Flexible, when the origin has a certificate. Flexible produced `SSL_ERROR_BAD_CERT_DOMAIN` and redirect loops after moving a domain to Cloudflare.
- **Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 renewal fails behind the proxy.** Switch to the DNS-01 challenge with a Cloudflare API token, or use a Cloudflare origin certificate, before the first renewal date.
- **Cache busting.** Depending on the zone's cache settings, `?v=N` on an asset may not create a new cache entry. If a fixed script does not reach browsers, purge the file or rename it, then confirm in the browser's network tab which version loaded. A stale cached script looks exactly like a server bug.
- Behind Cloudflare, the client IP is in `CF-Connecting-IP`. Include nginx's real-IP config before any IP blocklist or rate limit, and regenerate it when Cloudflare publishes new ranges, or every limit applies to Cloudflare's own addresses.
- When your backend hangs, Cloudflare answers with an HTML 504 page. A frontend that parses every response as JSON then shows "Unexpected token '<'". Check the status code before parsing, and treat this message as "the server hung", not as a frontend bug.

## 5. Frontend dependencies

- **Render-blocking third-party fonts take your login down with them.** During a Google outage, Firefox held the whole page on a Google Fonts stylesheet; mobile with cached fonts worked. Self-host fonts, or load them with the `media="print" onload` pattern.
- **`localStorage.setItem` can throw** (`QuotaExceededError`, private modes, full storage). One uncaught throw in the login flow showed users "The quota has been exceeded" and kept them out with a correct password. Use a helper that falls back to `sessionStorage`, then memory, and never throws. Do not show raw exception text in toasts.

## 6. Servers in general

- SSH by key only; root login and password auth off; a host firewall (ufw or nftables) on every box. A box that will hold a signer or a watcher key goes key-only before the key arrives.
- All boxes in UTC (`11-hot-keys-signers-watchers.md`, section 6).
- Backups: database dumps plus the files you cannot rebuild (`.env`, key files, uploaded user images), encrypted with one key you can store offline, copied off the box. Code comes back from git, so push every deploy; a commit that never reached the remote is not a backup.
- Before a kernel or package update that needs a reboot, list what must come back (process manager apps, systemd units, containers with restart policies) and check them after.
- Keep the node, the app and the watcher on separate boxes, so one provider problem does not take out the alert path together with the thing it watches.



<!-- FILE: 13-node-error-messages.md -->

# 13. Error messages, looked up

Paste the error, find it here, read the fix before changing anything. Every row is a real error from mainnet or testnet work, with the node's or tool's own words where known. Numbers in the messages vary; search for the fixed words.

**If you are an agent:** when a node refuses a transaction, find the message here before you rebuild. If it is not here, read the refusal against rusty-kaspa source before retrying with a different shape (`00-agent-rules.md`, "When to stop and ask").

## Node refusals (mempool and consensus)

| Message (fixed part) | What it means | Fix | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| `transaction input #0 has 21 signature operations which is more than the allowed max amount of 15` (`... is not standard`) | The P2SH redeem script holds more than 15 signature opcodes, counted without running it. Mempool policy; consensus and the script engine accept it, no public node relays it. | Select the key first, check once; merge entries with the same signers. | 03 §6 |
| `transaction storage mass of 800000 is larger than max allowed size of 500000` | An output is too small. Storage mass grows as one over the amount; covenant outputs with a covenant ID count four times. A covenant output under about 0.081 KAS cannot be created. | Raise the smallest output, or drop a tiny change output. | 02 §3 |
| `Storage mass exceeds maximum` (from the SDK while building) | You passed payout and change as explicit outputs plus a fee estimate, and the SDK added a third tiny change output. | One payment output, a change address, extra fee as `priorityFee`. For a full covenant spend, sweep. | 02 §4 |
| `transaction has N fees which is under the required amount of M for compute mass X` | Fee below the relay floor: 100 sompi per gram of max(compute, transient/2) since node v2.0.0 (it was 1 sompi per gram before). Common after the upgrade with old libraries and flat fees. | Compute the fee from mass. With legacy `@kaspa/wallet`, set `wallet.options.minimumRelayTransactionFee` right after creating the wallet (110000 is about 10% over the floor). The required amount in the message is exact; a retry can use it. | 02 §3 |
| `transaction input #0 is not finalized` | The transaction's `lockTime` is not strictly below the virtual DAA score while an input is not final. Setting `lockTime` to "now" causes it. | `lockTime` = now minus a small margin, still past the lock; wait a few blocks if needed. | 02 §4 |
| `failed to verify the signature script: Unsatisfied lock time: transaction input is finalized` | A CLTV path was spent with the input's sequence at MAX. The node then ignores `lockTime`, and the script refuses. | Set the input's sequence below MAX (0 is fine) on CLTV paths. | 02 §4 |
| `locktime requirement not satisfied -- locktime is greater than the transaction locktime: N > 0` | A relative (CSV) lock failed. The `0` is the input's sequence, not the transaction's lockTime. | Set the input's sequence to the lock value before signing. | 03 §3 |
| `sequence locks conditions was not met` | The coin is younger than the relative lock (an early spend), or a coin only a few DAA old was spent at once. The same transaction keeps the same id and is accepted later. | Wait until the coin's DAA score plus the lock is behind the virtual DAA; for fresh coins wait about 20 DAA. | 02 §4 |
| `Number too big ... 65 bytes which exceeds the max allowed of 8` | A pre-v1 multi-entry covenant read your signature as its entry selector. | Push the selector number after the arguments: `<sig> <selector> <redeem>`. | 02 §6, 03 §4 |
| `calculated contextual mass (including storage mass) X is not equal to the committed mass field Y` (node log, transaction inside a block) | Consensus WrongMass. Only applies to transactions arriving inside a block; over RPC the mempool overwrites the field. | Compute the mass with the node's own calculator when you build blocks or hand raw transactions to peers. | 02 §3 |
| A rejected transaction keeps the same id across attempts | You are submitting the same transaction (a fix did not reach the build, or a retry button re-sent the old signed copy). | Rebuild from scratch. | 02 §4 |

## Node and RPC behaviour

| Symptom | What it means | Fix | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reached connection capacity of 128` in `journalctl -u kaspad`; app sends stuck in "Full wallet sync" | The node's RPC client cap is full, by strangers or by your own leaked connections. | `--rpcmaxclients=1024` and/or a firewall; one shared connection per process. | 12 §1 |
| `Wallet sync timed out after 30s` | Same as above, or the client points at a seeder instead of a node. | Fix the connection leak; check the RPC endpoint constant. | 12 §1 |
| WebSocket client hangs forever, no error | Pointed at 16110 (gRPC). wRPC Borsh is 17110. | Use the right port. | 02 §2 |
| Connects, subscribes, then disconnects and reconnects in a loop | WASM SDK and node versions differ (Borsh framing is version-coupled). | Use the SDK from the node's release, or the JSON wRPC on 18110. | 12 §1 |
| Several `Connected` lines stacking up after reconnects | Every reconnect created a new `RpcClient` and the old one's listeners stayed bound. | Disconnect, remove listeners and drop the old client before creating a new one. | 02 §2 |
| `Failed to subscribe addresses: undefined` | Two things at once: the WASM SDK's `subscribeUtxosChanged` takes the address array itself, not `{ addresses }`, and the SDK throws strings, so `err.message` is undefined. | Pass the array; log `typeof err === 'string' ? err : err.message`. | 02 §2 |
| UTXO subscriptions silently never fire | Node started without `--utxoindex`. | Restart with `--utxoindex`. | 12 §1 |
| `rpc.disconnect()` crashes the Node process after a connect timeout | The racing connect promise rejected outside your try/catch. | Attach a no-op `.catch()` to it; skip disconnect when the timeout won. | 02 §2 |
| A token arrived but your wallet's UTXO subscription saw nothing | Token cells are P2SH coins that never touch the owner's address. | Learn arrivals from an indexer or from the virtual chain. | 05 §12 |

## SDK and wallet extensions

| Message or symptom | What it means | Fix | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| `... does not contain 'scriptPublicKey' property` | A hand-made UTXO entry used a plain `{version, script}` object. | `new ScriptPublicKey(0, bytes)`. | 02 §2 |
| `{...entry}` of a UTXO entry is empty | SDK entries are WASM class objects with getters. | Read the getters into a plain object yourself. | 02 §2 |
| Kasware: `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` on `signPskt` | Two-argument call. | One object: `{ txJsonString, options: { signInputs: [...] } }`. | 02 §5 |
| Kasware fails after the user signed | `autoFinalized: true` on a covenant input. | `autoFinalized: false`; assemble the signature script yourself. | 02 §5 |
| Kasware shows "Balance Change: 0" on a covenant spend | Normal: the input is not the wallet's own coin. | Tell the user in advance. | 01 §3 |
| Kastle returns the transaction with an empty P2SH signature, no error | Its dApp signer did not sign covenant inputs at the last test (Nov 2026). | Check every requested input for a signature before broadcast. | 02 §5 |
| Kaspire rejects at once | The wallet is locked; it does not open an unlock window. | Ask the user to unlock it. | 01 §3 |
| Signatures valid but useless on mainnet | Kasware was on the IGRA L2 network. | Check the wallet's network before every request. | 01 §3 |
| Server-side login check refuses every extension wallet after an update | `signMessage` changed format (base64 to hex; Kaspire returns an object). | Verify with the SDK's `verifyMessage` and accept all known shapes. | 02 §5 |

## Web stack

| Message or symptom | What it means | Fix | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Unexpected token '<'` / `... is not valid JSON` on a money call | The reverse proxy (often Cloudflare) returned an HTML 504 because the backend hung. | Find the hang (usually a node call without a timeout); check status codes before parsing JSON. | 12 §3, §4 |
| `The quota has been exceeded` toast at login | `localStorage.setItem` threw `QuotaExceededError`. | A storage helper that falls back and never throws. | 12 §5 |
| Page blank in one browser during a Google outage | Render-blocking Google Fonts stylesheet. | Self-host fonts. | 12 §5 |
| `SSL_ERROR_BAD_CERT_DOMAIN` after moving to Cloudflare | SSL mode Flexible. | Full (strict). | 12 §4 |
| A machine client gets an HTML challenge page from your API | The API hostname is proxied by Cloudflare. | DNS only for API and signer hosts. | 12 §4 |
| A fixed `.js` file keeps behaving like the old one | Long cache at nginx or the CDN; the query string may be ignored. | Purge or rename; confirm the loaded version in devtools. | 12 §4 |
| A new `.env` value is not used | The process never reloaded it, or `dotenv` ran after the module that reads it. | Restart fresh; load `dotenv` first; print the value at startup. | 12 §3 |
| Dates in the year 57,000 | Timestamps from api.kaspa.org (`block_time`) are already milliseconds; something multiplied by 1000. | Do not multiply. | 09 §5 |
| Alerts say "paused" or "stale" for one hour in autumn | A box not on UTC compared a MySQL `DATETIME` during the repeated DST hour. | UTC everywhere; compute ages in SQL. | 11 §6 |



<!-- FILE: 14-sdk-cookbook.md -->

# 14. SDK cookbook: the calls that actually work

Working call shapes for the rusty-kaspa WASM SDK (v2.1.0, Node.js build) and the `kaspa-ksm` covenant helper, taken from code that sends, signs and spends covenants on mainnet. Copy the shapes, keep the checks. When your SDK version differs, read its `kaspa.d.ts` before trusting any line here.

Everything in this file is **proven on mainnet** unless marked otherwise.

## 1. Getting the SDK

- Download `kaspa-wasm32-sdk-v<version>.zip` from the rusty-kaspa GitHub release that matches your node (`kaspad --version`). Never mix versions: the Borsh RPC framing changes between releases.
- Use the `nodejs/kaspa` folder in Node.js and the `web/kaspa` folder in browsers. Put it in your repo outside `node_modules` (for example `vendor/kaspa-wasm/`) and `require` it by path. A later `npm install` deletes anything you put inside `node_modules` by hand.
- The npm package named `kaspa` is a 2023 build (0.13.0) without covenant support. Do not use it for new work. Check any other npm package claiming to be the SDK before installing it; typosquats exist on every chain.
- In Node.js the SDK's RPC client needs a W3C WebSocket. Install the `websocket` npm package and set it once, before the first `RpcClient`:

```js
globalThis.WebSocket = require('websocket').w3cwebsocket;
const kaspa = require('./vendor/kaspa-wasm/nodejs/kaspa');
```

- The SDK throws plain strings, not `Error` objects. Wrap every catch:

```js
const errMsg = e => (typeof e === 'string' ? e : (e && e.message) || String(e));
```

- The zip contains `kaspa.d.ts`. When you are unsure of a function's name or argument shape, read it there. Do not guess from Bitcoin libraries or older Kaspa SDKs.

## 2. The pieces you need

| Need | SDK piece |
|---|---|
| Talk to a node | `RpcClient`, `Encoding` |
| A key to sign with | `PrivateKey` (from 32-byte hex) |
| Build and pay a normal KAS send | `createTransactions` (returns pending transactions with `.sign()` and `.submit()`) |
| Load, inspect, sign and serialize a transaction someone else built | `Transaction.deserializeFromSafeJSON`, `tx.serializeToSafeJSON()`, `tx.finalize()`, `tx.id`, `tx.inputs` |
| Sign one input with SIGHASH_ALL | `createInputSignature`, `SighashType.All` |
| Turn a script into an address | `ScriptPublicKey`, `addressFromScriptPublicKey` |
| Covenant files, spend plans, signature scripts | `kaspa-ksm` (npm): `verify`, `planSpend`, `applyPlan`, `signatureScript` / `finalize` |
| Compile SilverScript | `silverc` binary, pinned to one commit (`03-silverscript-v1-gotchas.md`) |

That is the whole list for sending, signing, covenant spends and reading coins. Anything else, look up in `kaspa.d.ts` first.

## 3. Connecting to a node

```js
const NETWORK = 'mainnet';                      // or 'testnet-10'
const NODE = process.env.KASPA_BORSH || null;   // your own node, e.g. 'ws://127.0.0.1:17110'; unset = public nodes

function withTimeout(p, ms, label) {
  let t;
  return Promise.race([p, new Promise((_, rej) => { t = setTimeout(() => rej(new Error(`${label} timed out`)), ms); })])
    .finally(() => clearTimeout(t));
}

async function withRpc(fn) {
  const rpc = NODE
    ? new kaspa.RpcClient({ url: NODE, encoding: kaspa.Encoding.Borsh, networkId: NETWORK })   // your own node
    : new kaspa.RpcClient({ resolver: new kaspa.Resolver(), networkId: NETWORK });               // a public node
  await withTimeout(rpc.connect(), 20000, 'node connect');
  try {
    const info = await rpc.getInfo();
    if (!info.isSynced) throw new Error('node not synced');
    if (!info.isUtxoIndexed) throw new Error('node started without --utxoindex');
    return await fn(rpc);
  } finally {
    try { await rpc.disconnect(); } catch (_) { /* already closed */ }
  }
}
```

- Without `KASPA_BORSH` set, the SDK's `Resolver` picks a public node (the pattern of rusty-kaspa's own examples). That is enough for apps whose server holds no key (`00-agent-rules.md`, "How strict to be"). Set your own node when the server signs or watches.
- 17110 is wRPC Borsh, 16110 is gRPC. A WebSocket client pointed at 16110 hangs with no error.
- A short-lived client per operation (as above) is fine for occasional sends. A busy service keeps one long-lived client per process instead (section 9). Never one per request without a `disconnect()`; that fills the node's client cap.
- Put a timeout on every call. A call that never returns will hold up everything queued behind it.

## 4. Reading coins and the chain clock

```js
// Unspent coins at one or more addresses. Note: an object with `addresses` here.
const { entries } = await rpc.getUtxosByAddresses({ addresses: [address] });

// Field paths differ slightly between builds; normalize once.
function coinOf(e) {
  const u = (e && (e.utxoEntry || e.entry)) || e;
  const op = (e && e.outpoint) || u.outpoint;
  return {
    txid: String(op.transactionId).toLowerCase(),
    vout: Number(op.index),
    amount: BigInt(u.amount),                 // sompi, BigInt
    daa: BigInt(u.blockDaaScore),             // DAA score of the block that accepted it
    covenantId: u.covenantId ? String(u.covenantId) : null,
    raw: e,                                   // pass this unchanged to createTransactions
  };
}

// The chain's clock, for lockTime and relative locks
const { virtualDaaScore } = await rpc.getBlockDagInfo();
```

- Amounts are BigInt sompi. Never convert to `Number` before summing.
- A coin at a plain `kaspa:q` address that carries a `covenantId` is not plain KAS (it is a token cell or similar). Do not spend it as KAS.
- Keep `raw` and hand it to `createTransactions` as is. A hand-made entry needs a real `new kaspa.ScriptPublicKey(0, hex)`, not a `{version, script}` object.

## 5. Sending KAS from a key you hold

```js
async function sendKas(rpc, privKeyHex, fromAddress, payments /* [{address, amount: BigInt}] */) {
  const { entries } = await rpc.getUtxosByAddresses({ addresses: [fromAddress] });
  const total = payments.reduce((a, p) => a + p.amount, 0n);
  const available = entries.reduce((a, e) => a + BigInt(coinOf(e).amount), 0n);
  if (available - total < 5_000_000n) throw new Error('keep at least 0.05 KAS for the fee');

  const { transactions, summary } = await kaspa.createTransactions({
    entries,
    outputs: payments,                  // every output paid exactly
    changeAddress: fromAddress,         // change comes back to the sender
    priorityFee: 0n,                    // the SDK adds the mass-based fee itself
    networkId: NETWORK,
  });

  const key = new kaspa.PrivateKey(privKeyHex);
  const submitted = [];
  try {
    for (const pending of transactions) {       // may be several: consolidations first, payment last
      await pending.sign([key]);
      submitted.push(String(await pending.submit(rpc)));
    }
  } catch (e) {
    // Something may already be on the network. Report it; never retry blind.
    e.submitted = submitted;
    throw e;
  }
  return { txid: String(summary.finalTransactionId || submitted.at(-1)), txids: submitted, feeSompi: BigInt(summary.fees || 0) };
}
```

- Before signing with a key you derived from a seed, derive its address and compare it with the address you expect to spend from. Refuse on a mismatch.
- If the user wants "send everything", that is a different call shape (no outputs, `changeAddress` = destination). Never let a normal payment fall into a sweep.
- Map node errors to plain words: "storage mass" means an amount is too small; "insufficient" means not enough to cover amount plus fee. Full list: `13-node-error-messages.md`.

## 6. Signing a transaction someone else built (PSKT / SafeJSON)

The format browser wallets and apps exchange is the SDK's "safe JSON" of a transaction, plus a list of `{ index, sighashType }` to sign.

```js
function signInputs(txJsonString, privKeyHex, indexes) {
  const tx = kaspa.Transaction.deserializeFromSafeJSON(txJsonString);   // throws if it is not a transaction
  const key = new kaspa.PrivateKey(privKeyHex);
  for (const i of indexes) {
    const sig = String(kaspa.createInputSignature(tx, i, key, kaspa.SighashType.All)).toLowerCase();
    if (!/^41[0-9a-f]{128}01$/.test(sig)) throw new Error(`unexpected signature shape on input ${i}`);
    tx.inputs[i].signatureScript = sig;      // a push of the 64-byte Schnorr signature plus the sighash byte
  }
  const signed = tx.serializeToSafeJSON();

  // Only signature scripts may differ from what you were given
  const a = JSON.parse(txJsonString), b = JSON.parse(signed);
  if (a.inputs.length !== b.inputs.length || a.outputs.length !== b.outputs.length ||
      String(a.lockTime) !== String(b.lockTime) ||
      a.outputs.some((o, n) => String(o.value) !== String(b.outputs[n].value))) {
    throw new Error('transaction changed during signing');
  }
  return signed;
}
```

- `SighashType.All` only, for anything that came from outside your own code (`01-wallet-safety.md`).
- For a P2PK input, `41<sig>01` is the complete signature script. For a covenant input it is one argument; the app adds the other arguments, the dispatch tag and the redeem script (section 8).
- Before signing coins the app says are the user's, look each outpoint up on a node you trust (section 4) and compare amount and script. Refuse if anything differs.
- If you sign for other apps, sign and return. Do not broadcast for them.

## 7. Broadcasting a finished transaction

```js
async function broadcast(rpc, txJsonString) {
  const tx = kaspa.Transaction.deserializeFromSafeJSON(txJsonString);
  tx.finalize();                                   // the id is only right after finalize()
  const expected = String(tx.id).toLowerCase();
  try {
    const res = await rpc.submitTransaction({ transaction: tx, allowOrphan: false });
    return String((res && res.transactionId) || expected).toLowerCase();
  } catch (e) {
    const msg = errMsg(e);
    if (msg.includes(expected) && /already in the mempool|already accepted/i.test(msg)) return expected;  // a retry of a success
    throw new Error(msg);
  }
}
```

- The transaction id does not cover signature scripts, so you know it before signing. If a rejected transaction keeps the same id on every retry, you are sending the same transaction; rebuild.
- `allowOrphan: false` unless you deliberately build on an output that is not yet accepted.

## 8. Spending a covenant coin (one coin in, one output out)

The shape that works on mainnet: plan the path with `kaspa-ksm`, build a **sweep** with the SDK, check it, write the lock fields, sign, assemble the signature script, broadcast.

```js
const ksm = require('kaspa-ksm');

async function spendCovenantCoin(rpc, { manifest, entry, args, coin, destination, keys /* {sigParam: privHex} */, maxFeeSompi }) {
  const check = ksm.verify(manifest);
  if (!check.ok) throw new Error('covenant file does not verify: ' + check.errors.join('; '));

  const { virtualDaaScore } = await rpc.getBlockDagInfo();
  const plan = ksm.planSpend(manifest, entry, {
    args: args || {},
    chain: { daa: virtualDaaScore, nowMs: Date.now() },
    utxos: [{ blockDaaScore: coin.daa.toString() }],
  });
  if (!plan.ready) throw new Error('not spendable yet: ' + plan.blockers.join('; '));
  const dest = plan.payTo ? plan.payTo.address : destination;    // a path that pins its payee wins

  // The SDK sizes the fee without the signature script it cannot see; add it as priority fee
  const sigScriptBytes = plan.layout.reduce((n, x) => n + (x.kind === 'sig' ? 66 : x.hex.length / 2), 0)
                       + plan.suffixHex.length / 2;
  let priority = (BigInt(sigScriptBytes) + 64n) * 100n;
  if (priority < 20000n) priority = 20000n;

  // Sweep: no outputs, change goes to the destination
  const settings = { entries: [coin.raw], outputs: [], changeAddress: dest, priorityFee: priority, networkId: NETWORK };
  let built;
  try { built = await kaspa.createTransactions(settings); }
  catch (_) { delete settings.outputs; built = await kaspa.createTransactions(settings); }   // some builds want it absent
  if (built.transactions.length !== 1) throw new Error('expected exactly one transaction');
  const unsignedJson = built.transactions[0].serializeToSafeJSON();

  // Check before anyone signs: one in, one out, to the right address, fee within the covenant's cap
  const raw = JSON.parse(unsignedJson);
  if (raw.inputs.length !== 1 || raw.outputs.length !== 1) throw new Error('not a one-in-one-out spend');
  const spk = raw.outputs[0].scriptPublicKey;
  const outHex = String(typeof spk === 'string' ? spk : spk.script).toLowerCase().replace(/^0000/, '');
  const outAddr = kaspa.addressFromScriptPublicKey(new kaspa.ScriptPublicKey(0, outHex), NETWORK).toString();
  if (outAddr !== dest) throw new Error(`output pays ${outAddr}, expected ${dest}`);
  const fee = coin.amount - BigInt(raw.outputs[0].value);
  if (fee <= 0n || fee > maxFeeSompi) throw new Error(`fee ${fee} outside the covenant's cap`);

  // sequence, lockTime and sigOpCount go in BEFORE signing; they are all in the signature hash
  const txJson = ksm.applyPlan(plan, unsignedJson);

  const tx = kaspa.Transaction.deserializeFromSafeJSON(txJson);
  const sigs = {};
  for (const name of plan.signaturesNeeded) {
    const s = String(kaspa.createInputSignature(tx, 0, new kaspa.PrivateKey(keys[name]), kaspa.SighashType.All)).toLowerCase();
    if (!/^41[0-9a-f]{128}01$/.test(s)) throw new Error(`unexpected signature shape for ${name}`);
    sigs[name] = s;
  }
  const signed = JSON.parse(txJson);
  signed.inputs[0].signatureScript = ksm.signatureScript(plan, sigs);   // <args> <dispatch tag> <redeem script>
  return broadcast(rpc, JSON.stringify(signed));
}
```

- **Why a sweep:** asking the SDK for a fixed output plus change on a covenant spend leaves the difference between your fee estimate and the SDK's as a tiny change output, and the node refuses it on storage mass. `kaspa-ksm`'s own `buildSpendTx` helper (checked in 1.3.0, Nov 2026) builds that fixed-output-plus-change shape; use `planSpend`, `applyPlan` and `signatureScript` from its core with your own sweep, as above.
- Measured: a small single-signature covenant spend costs about 0.0019 KAS this way.
- **Exact amounts from a sweep** (an invite that must deliver exactly 5 KAS): build once, read the SDK's base fee (`fee - priority`), rebuild with `priority = (coin.amount - wanted) - baseFee` so the single output lands on the wanted value. The surplus becomes fee, never a second output. Rebuild once more if storage mass moved the base fee.
- **Partial withdrawals** (part leaves, the rest stays in the covenant): one payment output, `changeAddress` = the covenant's own address, extra fee as `priorityFee`. The change coin's relative age starts again at zero.
- When the user signs in a browser wallet instead of your server, send `txJson` (after `applyPlan`) to the wallet's `signPskt`, take the `41<sig>01` it returns for each input, and assemble the same way (`02-sending-and-signing-kas.md` section 5 has the wallet calls).
- An early spend of a relative lock is refused with "sequence locks conditions was not met". The same transaction, unchanged, is accepted once the coin is old enough.

## 9. Following addresses live

```js
class Follower {
  async connect(addresses) {
    if (this.rpc) {                                   // dispose the old client, or listeners stack up
      try { await this.rpc.disconnect(); } catch (_) {}
      try { this.rpc.removeAllListeners?.(); } catch (_) {}
      this.rpc = null;
    }
    const rpc = this.rpc = NODE
      ? new kaspa.RpcClient({ url: NODE, encoding: kaspa.Encoding.Borsh, networkId: NETWORK })
      : new kaspa.RpcClient({ resolver: new kaspa.Resolver(), networkId: NETWORK });

    // Register listeners BEFORE connecting and subscribing. Payloads arrive under event.data.
    rpc.addEventListener('connect', () => { this.connected = true; });
    rpc.addEventListener('disconnect', () => { this.connected = false; this.scheduleReconnect(addresses); });
    rpc.addEventListener('utxos-changed', ev => this.onUtxos(ev.data));            // { added: [...], removed: [...] }
    rpc.addEventListener('virtual-daa-score-changed', ev => { this.daa = BigInt(ev.data.virtualDaaScore); });

    await rpc.connect();
    const info = await rpc.getInfo();
    if (!info.isUtxoIndexed) throw new Error('node needs --utxoindex');
    await rpc.subscribeVirtualDaaScoreChanged();
    await rpc.subscribeUtxosChanged(addresses);       // the array itself, not { addresses }
  }
}
```

- One payment fires several `utxos-changed` events in a burst. Serialize balance updates per wallet, or you will report the same receipt twice.
- Re-read the balance from the node after events; do not add up event deltas forever.
- Public explorer APIs lag the node push. If you also fetch history from one after an event, retry for a few seconds before concluding nothing arrived.
- Token arrivals do not show up here (`05-kcc20-tokens.md` section 12).
- Reconnect with backoff, and re-subscribe every address after each reconnect.

## 10. Units and addresses

```js
const SOMPI = 100_000_000n;

function kasToSompi(text) {                         // "2.5" -> 250000000n, exactly
  const m = /^(\d+)(?:\.(\d{1,8}))?$/.exec(String(text).trim());
  if (!m) throw new Error('amount must be KAS with up to 8 decimals');
  return BigInt(m[1]) * SOMPI + BigInt((m[2] || '').padEnd(8, '0'));
}

function sompiToKas(sompi) {                        // 250000000n -> "2.50000000"
  const s = BigInt(sompi);
  return `${s / SOMPI}.${(s % SOMPI).toString().padStart(8, '0')}`;
}

// Address from a script, e.g. an output's scriptPublicKey (strip a leading 0000 version if present)
const addr = kaspa.addressFromScriptPublicKey(new kaspa.ScriptPublicKey(0, scriptHex), NETWORK).toString();
```

- Convert between KAS and sompi in exactly one place. Users type KAS; scripts and the SDK take sompi.
- Script shapes you will meet: P2PK Schnorr `20<32-byte key>ac` (`kaspa:q…`), P2PK ECDSA `21<33-byte key>ab`, P2SH `aa20<32-byte hash>87` (`kaspa:p…`). Inside a covenant script they carry a `0000` version prefix.
- Do not write your own bech32 for Kaspa addresses; use the SDK.

## 11. Legacy `@kaspa/wallet`

Older code derives keys and sends with the gRPC wallet SDK `@kaspa/wallet`. It still works, but:

- Set `wallet.options.minimumRelayTransactionFee = 110000` right after `Wallet.fromMnemonic(...)` on every wallet instance. Its default predates the current fee floor by a factor of 100.
- Reuse one gRPC connection per process and close what you open.
- For anything with covenants or the newer transaction fields, use the WASM SDK. Keys derived with `@kaspa/wallet` can sign through the WASM SDK as `new kaspa.PrivateKey(hex)`; check the derived address first.



<!-- FILE: 15-multi-wallet-support.md -->

# 15. Supporting several wallets

How to let users connect with whichever Kaspa wallet they have: browser extensions (Kasware, Kaspire, Kastle), hosted web wallets (Kasla and similar) and phone wallets (Kasanova, Kurncy and others). Every call below is taken from wallet-connect code running in production on mainnet (Nov 2026) unless marked **practice**. Wallets update often: when one stops behaving as described, check its current docs and say so in an issue here.

Read with `01-wallet-safety.md` (what can go wrong) and `02-sending-and-signing-kas.md` section 5 (the send and sign call shapes).

## 1. The shape: one adapter per wallet

Write one small object per wallet with the same methods, and never branch on wallet names in the rest of the app.

```js
// Every adapter answers the same questions. `can` decides what the UI offers.
// { id, label, detect(), connect() -> address, activeAddress(), onAccountChange(fn),
//   signMessage(msg) -> signature, sendKas(to, sompi) -> txid, signPskt(txJsonString, indexes),
//   can: { send, signMessage, signCovenant } }
```

| Wallet | Kind | Send KAS | Sign a message (login) | Sign a covenant input |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kasware | extension | yes | yes | yes (`signPskt`) |
| Kaspire | extension, request-style | yes | yes (returns an object) | yes (`signPskt` with `sender`) |
| Kastle | extension | yes | yes | **no** at the last test (Nov 2026): it returns the transaction with the covenant input unsigned, and no error |
| Hosted web wallet (Kasla) | no extension; login by redirect | yes, through an approval page on the wallet's site | no; login is an OAuth-style redirect | yes, through a signing-request approval page; the wallet never broadcasts |
| Phone wallets (Kasanova, Kurncy) | separate app | the user sends by scanning an address | no page connection | no |

Offer only what a wallet can do on this page. A page that must sign covenant spends hides Kastle (or explains it) instead of letting the user reach the last step and fail.

## 2. Detection

```js
const hasKasware = () => typeof window.kasware !== 'undefined';
const hasKastle  = () => typeof window.kastle !== 'undefined';
const hasKaspire = () => typeof window.kaspire !== 'undefined' && window.kaspire !== null && window.kaspire.isKaspire === true;
const isMobile   = () => /Android|iPhone|iPad|iPod/i.test(navigator.userAgent);
```

- Check when the user clicks Connect, not only at page load: extensions inject their object at their own pace.
- Desktop extensions do not exist in phone browsers. On a phone, offer the hosted wallet and the QR flow (section 7), not extension buttons that cannot work.
- Kaspire is a request-style provider: one `request({ method, params })` instead of named methods.

```js
function kaspireRequest(method, params) {
  const req = { method };
  if (params !== undefined) req.params = params;
  return window.kaspire.request(req);
}
```

## 3. Connecting (getting the address)

Ask silently first, prompt only if needed.

```js
async function connectKasware() {
  let accounts = await window.kasware.getAccounts().catch(() => []);
  if (!accounts.length) accounts = await window.kasware.requestAccounts();   // shows the wallet's prompt
  let address = accounts[0];
  if (address && !address.startsWith('kaspa:')) address = 'kaspa:' + address; // normalize
  return address;
}

async function connectKastle() {
  await window.kastle.connect('mainnet');            // the network is part of the connect call
  const account = await window.kastle.getAccount();
  return account.address;
}

async function connectKaspire() {
  let accounts = await kaspireRequest('getAccounts').catch(() => []);
  if (!accounts || !accounts.length) accounts = await kaspireRequest('requestAccounts');
  const address = accounts && accounts[0];
  if (typeof address !== 'string' || !address.startsWith('kaspa:')) {
    throw new Error('Switch Kaspire to Kaspa Mainnet and try again');   // a testnet address starts kaspatest:
  }
  return address;
}
```

- **Kaspire rejects at once when it is locked**; it does not open an unlock window. Tell the user to unlock it.
- **The network.** Kastle takes it in `connect`. For Kaspire, the address prefix tells mainnet (`kaspa:`) from testnet (`kaspatest:`). Kasware can be switched to the IGRA L2, and the address alone does not show that. The production code does not call a network API for Kasware; it tells the user to check the network name in the wallet before signing (`01-wallet-safety.md` section 3).

## 4. Login: sign a challenge, verify on the server

A connected address proves nothing. Login is a signature over a one-time challenge your server issued.

```js
// 1. server: issue a nonce for this address and this site
const { nonce } = await (await fetch('/api/auth/nonce', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ address, site: location.origin }) })).json();

// 2. the wallet signs it
let signature;
if (walletId === 'kasware') signature = await window.kasware.signMessage(nonce);
if (walletId === 'kastle')  signature = await window.kastle.signMessage(nonce);
if (walletId === 'kaspire') {
  const r = await kaspireRequest('signMessage', { address, message: nonce });
  signature = r && r.signature ? r.signature : r;            // Kaspire returns { address, signature }
}

// 3. server: verify, then issue a session
await fetch('/api/auth/connect', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ address, message: nonce, signature, walletType: walletId, site: location.origin }) });
```

Server side:

- Verify with the SDK's `verifyMessage` against the 32-byte key carried in the `kaspa:q…` address. Accept every signature shape seen: Kasware 0.11.0 returns 128 hex characters, older Kasware 88 characters of base64, Kaspire an object (unwrap `.signature`). Proven on mainnet after a Kasware update broke a login that accepted only one shape.
- **Practice:** a nonce is single-use, expires in minutes, and is bound to the site it was issued for. Put the site's origin in the signed text so a signature from one site cannot log into another.
- Issue a session token (a signed JWT, for example) and verify it on every request that touches money. The address in the verified token is the user; never an address the browser sends later (`02-sending-and-signing-kas.md` section 7).

## 5. Keep the session on the wallet's account

```js
async function activeAddress(walletId) {
  if (walletId === 'kasware') { const a = await window.kasware.getAccounts(); return (a && a[0]) || null; }
  if (walletId === 'kastle')  { const i = await window.kastle.getAccount();   return (i && i.address) || null; }
  if (walletId === 'kaspire') { const a = await kaspireRequest('getAccounts'); return (a && a[0]) || null; }
  return null;
}

function watchAccountSwitch(onSwitch) {
  const h = accounts => onSwitch(Array.isArray(accounts) ? accounts[0] : (accounts && accounts.address) || null);
  try { if (window.kasware && typeof window.kasware.on === 'function') window.kasware.on('accountsChanged', h); } catch (_) {}
  try { if (window.kastle && typeof window.kastle.on === 'function') window.kastle.on('accountsChanged', h); } catch (_) {}
  try { if (hasKaspire() && typeof window.kaspire.on === 'function') window.kaspire.on('accountsChanged', h); } catch (_) {}
}
```

- On an account switch, end the session and reconnect.
- Before every signature, compare `activeAddress()` with the session's address and refuse on a mismatch. A real payout once went to the wrong party because the extension had switched accounts after login (`08-failures-log.md`, Wallets).

## 6. Hosted web wallets (no extension)

A hosted wallet (Kasla is one) holds the user's key on its own servers, so there is nothing in the page to call. Two flows:

**Login by redirect.** Your page sends the user to the wallet's connect URL with a return address; the wallet sends them back with a token.

- **Practice:** before redirecting, store a random `state` value in `sessionStorage` and send it along; on return, refuse a token that does not come back with the same `state`. Otherwise anyone can send a user a link that logs them into the attacker's account.
- Verify the returned token on your server (or with the wallet's verify endpoint) before treating the user as logged in, and remove the token from the address bar at once (`history.replaceState`). Prefer a token in the URL fragment (`#`) over the query string, which ends up in server logs.

**Payments and signatures by approval page.** Your server creates the request with the wallet (payee, amount, memo, or a transaction to sign with the input indexes), gets back an approval URL, and the page opens it.

- Open the popup inside the click handler (`window.open` first, then point it at the URL), or the browser blocks it.
- The user approves on the wallet's own site. Your page learns the result by polling the request's status for the transaction id.
- For a signing request the wallet returns the signed transaction and never broadcasts; your code assembles any covenant signature script and broadcasts it.

## 7. Phone wallets and "any wallet"

A phone wallet cannot be called from a desktop page, and most cannot tell a page which address they control.

- Show the receiving address as a QR code and as text with a copy button, and show the exact amount in KAS beside it. **Practice:** encode the plain address in the QR. No Kaspa payment-link format with an amount was found that wallets agree on, so do not count on an amount inside the QR.
- Learn that the payment arrived by watching the address (`16-accepting-payments.md`). To tell orders apart, give each order its own address, or a slightly different amount.
- If you must route such payments into a per-user covenant, one working pattern is a one-time intake address that your server forwards from within seconds. That makes your server briefly custodial (it holds the intake key): say so to users, and treat it under the third row of the tiers in `00-agent-rules.md`.

## 8. If you would rather not build this

A hosted connect widget already does detection, login and the hosted-wallet flow for Kasware, Kastle, Kaspire and Kasla (KasperoConnect, served by kasperopay.com, with a merchant id from its operator). Using one is a trust decision: the widget's operator issues your users' sessions.

## 9. Test each wallet before you list it

- A fresh browser profile with only that wallet installed.
- The wallet locked; the user rejecting the prompt; the user closing the popup.
- The wrong network (testnet, IGRA).
- Switching accounts after login, then trying to pay.
- A phone, and a popup blocker.
- One real send and, if the page needs it, one real covenant signature on mainnet with a tiny amount.



<!-- FILE: 16-accepting-payments.md -->

# 16. Accepting a KAS payment

The most common thing people build: a shop, a tip jar, a paywall, a ticket. This is the second row of the tiers in `00-agent-rules.md`: the payer's wallet signs, your server holds no key, and public nodes or the REST API are enough. Lines marked **practice** are recommendations, not chain facts.

## 1. The rule everything else follows

**An order is paid when a node shows the coin at your address, never when the browser says so.** A page can report any txid it likes. Check the chain yourself: the right address, at least the right amount, accepted.

## 2. Your receiving address

- Receive to an address whose key your server does not hold (a wallet the merchant controls). Then a breach of the web server cannot spend the takings.
- **Telling orders apart.** Pick one:
  - **One address per order.** Cleanest. Derive receive addresses from the merchant wallet's extended public key on the server, so no spending key is involved (check your SDK version for the call), or let the merchant's wallet hand out fresh receive addresses.
  - **One address, a unique amount per order** (add a few sompi: 25.00000137 KAS). Simple for a small shop. Expire the amount with the order, and match on the exact value.
  - **A covenant per order** (an escrow, `04-covenant-design-patterns.md`) when the money should wait for delivery or allow a refund.
- Do not reuse one address with the same amount for everyone; you cannot tell who paid.

## 3. Taking the payment

**A. Extension wallet on the page.** The wallet sends; your server checks.

```js
// browser
const txid = await window.kasware.sendKaspa(order.address, Number(order.amountSompi), {});
await fetch('/api/orders/' + order.id + '/paid', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ txid }) });     // a hint for the server, not proof
```

Other wallets' send calls: `02-sending-and-signing-kas.md` section 5 and `15-multi-wallet-support.md`.

**B. Any wallet, by QR.** Show the address (as a QR and as text) and the exact amount. Watch the address until the coin arrives or the order expires (section 4).

**C. Hosted web wallet.** Create the payment request with the wallet's API, open its approval page inside the click, and poll for the txid (`15-multi-wallet-support.md` section 6). Then check it like any other payment.

## 4. Checking it on the server

With a node (yours, or a public one through the `Resolver`; `14-sdk-cookbook.md` sections 3 and 4):

```js
async function isPaid(rpc, order, txidHint) {
  const { entries } = await rpc.getUtxosByAddresses({ addresses: [order.address] });
  const coins = entries.map(coinOf).filter(c => !c.covenantId);           // plain KAS only, not token cells
  const match = txidHint
    ? coins.find(c => c.txid === String(txidHint).toLowerCase())
    : coins.find(c => c.amount === BigInt(order.amountSompi));             // unique-amount orders
  if (!match) return { paid: false };
  if (match.amount < BigInt(order.amountSompi)) return { paid: false, short: match.amount };
  return { paid: true, txid: match.txid, amount: match.amount, daa: match.daa };
}
```

- This works while the coin is unspent at the address, which is the case for a receiving address the merchant does not sweep every second.
- Or use the REST API: `GET https://api.kaspa.org/transactions/<txid>` and check that one output pays your address the amount and that the transaction is accepted. Field names are in api.kaspa.org/docs; times there are already milliseconds.
- Follow many orders with `subscribeUtxosChanged` on their addresses instead of polling (`14-sdk-cookbook.md` section 9). For a few orders, polling every few seconds is fine.

**How long to wait (practice).** On mainnet a transaction is accepted within a second or two. For small amounts, accepted is enough. For larger ones, wait a little longer before releasing goods: a reorg deep enough to undo an accepted payment is rare, and the cost of waiting a few more seconds is low. One indexer in production waits 100 confirmations, about 10 seconds at 10 blocks per second.

## 5. Order rules (practice)

- **Quote in KAS, lock it.** If prices are in dollars, convert once at checkout, show the KAS amount, and give the quote a lifetime (10 to 15 minutes). Name the price source (`12-nodes-and-servers.md` section 1).
- **Underpaid:** do not mark paid; show what is missing; let the payer top up to the same address or amount before expiry.
- **Overpaid:** mark paid and record the excess for a manual refund.
- **Late:** a payment after expiry still arrived. Record it and handle it by hand; never lose it silently.
- **One payment, one order.** Store the txid and refuse to attach it to a second order.
- **The payer pays the network fee.** Ask for the exact amount to arrive.
- **Exchanges.** Some refuse to withdraw to a covenant (`kaspa:p…`) address, and their payouts arrive from addresses that are not the customer's. Do not refund to the sender address of an exchange payment; ask for a refund address.
- **Webhooks** to the merchant's system are signed (HMAC, constant-time compare, short timestamp window).

## 6. Tokens (KCC-20)

Token payments do not show up on the receiving address: a token coin is a covenant coin with its own address. Learn them from a KCC-20 indexer or by following the chain (`05-kcc20-tokens.md` section 12), and identify the token by its covenant ID, never by its name.

## 7. What to tell the merchant

- "Your shop page never holds your wallet's key. Money goes straight to your wallet."
- "An order counts as paid when the network shows the payment, not when the customer's browser says so."
- "Refunds are manual: you send them from your wallet."



<!-- FILE: 17-token-launchers.md -->

# 17. Building a token launcher

Practices for any site or tool that lets people create KCC-20 tokens. Learned from running a launcher on mainnet through the KCC-20 launch (Oct 2026) and from indexing every other launcher's tokens. Read with `05-kcc20-tokens.md` (how tokens work on chain) and `06-redteam-before-deploy.md`.

A launcher is where most token scams start: a copied name, a hostile string in metadata, an icon that is really a page. Everything a launcher accepts will be shown by wallets and explorers you do not control. Treat every field as an attack on them.

## 1. Names and tickers

- **Normalize before comparing:** Unicode NFKC, Cyrillic and Greek lookalikes folded to Latin, digit swaps (0/O, 1/I, 5/S), accents dropped, letters and digits only. Compare that "skeleton", never the raw string. `NАCHO` with a Cyrillic А is `NACHO`.
- **Reserved names are refused:** the majors (Bitcoin, Kaspa, Ethereum, wrapped assets), stablecoin names (USD, USDT, USDC and bridged variants), and existing community tokens from earlier Kaspa token standards. Keep the list in a file you can extend without a deploy, and check names, tickers and words inside names. Publishing your list lets other launchers reuse it.
- **First come, first served:** a name already launched is refused for everyone except its original launcher, who may launch numbered siblings (`PRIZE1`, then `PRIZE2`).
- **Refuse names that cannot be told apart from nothing:** whitespace-only or punctuation-only names (a token named `" "` was launched), names with no letter at all, and names that look like an indexer's placeholder for an unnamed token (`Token 1a2b3c4d`, `STD-…`).
- **Refuse without saying which rule matched.** "This name is not available" is enough; a detailed reason teaches a scammer which character to change.
- Strip and refuse control characters, zero-width characters and right-to-left override characters in names and tickers. They let `TOKEN` and `NEKOT` look alike on screen.

## 2. Every other open field

- The safest launcher has no free-text fields beyond name and ticker. One launcher dropped description and website before launch day because they were attack vectors that helped neither wallets nor indexers.
- If you keep them: plain text only, a length cap per field, HTML and markdown stripped (not escaped and stored; stripped), control, zero-width and bidi characters removed, and URLs limited to `https://` with a host. Store what you accepted, not what was sent.
- Remember the reader: wallets and explorers will render these strings with code you did not write. Assume one of them does not escape HTML. What you refuse at the door is the only protection their users get from you.
- On your own pages, show links from metadata as text, never as clickable links.

## 3. Images

- A size cap on upload (a few MB), then **decode and re-encode** to one raster format at a fixed square size, with metadata stripped. Never store the original bytes.
- **Never accept, store or serve SVG.** It can carry script. Read the file type from the bytes, never from the name or a `data:` header (a `data:image/html` upload once became stored XSS on a wallet's own domain).
- Decide on animated images before launch. One launcher found animated icons annoying in wallets and was still undecided; whatever you choose, make it a rule.
- Pin the image by its hash. Put the hash (or the image) in the on-chain metadata at genesis, so anyone can check that the picture a wallet shows is the one the launcher committed to.

## 4. What goes on chain

- **Metadata at genesis** (KCC-23: in the transaction the genesis's authorizing input spends), with the image hash. No links that an indexer must fetch, no off-chain registration step.
- Anything you want to prove about a launch (an endowment, an allocation, a fee paid) goes in the genesis transaction itself, where everyone can read it.
- **A unique value in every per-token covenant** (the token's covenant ID, for example). Two launches with the same terms otherwise produce the same script and the same address: two test tokens once shared one miner-drip covenant.

## 5. The program and its powers

- **Use the pinned reference KCC-20 build** unless you have a reason not to. Wallets and indexers read it; a variant of your own is invisible to them until they pin it (`05-kcc20-tokens.md` section 2).
- **No issuer powers by default.** A launcher should not hand a token's creator the power to freeze, burn, seize or mint on holders' coins. If a token type has such powers by design (a regulated stablecoin), the launch page and the token page say so up front.
- **Red-team every covenant your launcher deploys** (pools, curves, drips, minters, sale contracts). A keyless drip used at launch shipped on mainnet without `require(tx.inputs.length == 1)`; two equal coins could be merged and the second paid to the miner (`08-failures-log.md`).
- Publish your programs' source, or at least their template hashes, so indexers can recognize and label your tokens.

## 6. The launch flow

- Show the full cost before the signature: network fees, any platform fee, any endowment, the KAS each token coin carries.
- Say "launched" only after a node shows the genesis accepted and the covenant ID exists.
- Tell launchers plainly that a wallet shows a new token only once its indexer reads the token's program and metadata. A token can be real and still invisible in a wallet for a while.
- Keep a launch record (genesis txid, covenant ID, metadata, image hash) the launcher can download.

## 7. Spam and junk

- A free launcher gets flooded. A launch fee or a deposit filters out "let's launch 1,000 tokens and see". Weigh the price against honest small launchers.
- Expect test tokens. Name them clearly on your own pages, or ask launchers to use testnet. Indexers filter names like "test" and tokens whose supply sits at a burn address; make that easy for them.

## 8. Checklist

- [ ] Names and tickers checked by skeleton against the reserved list and every launched name; numbered siblings only for the original launcher.
- [ ] Whitespace-only, letterless, placeholder-looking and invisible-character names refused, with no reason shown.
- [ ] Free-text fields dropped, or plain text with caps, stripped of HTML and invisible characters, URLs `https://` only.
- [ ] Images re-encoded to a fixed raster, typed from their bytes, SVG refused, hash pinned on chain.
- [ ] Metadata and image hash in the genesis; per-token covenants carry a unique value.
- [ ] Reference build, no hidden issuer powers, every launch covenant red-teamed.
- [ ] Full cost shown before signing; "launched" only after the node shows the genesis.
